title: Position: Generative Engine Optimization Creates Underexamined Risks, Governance Must Target Concentration, Disclosure, and Academic Blind Spots
claim: Traditional ranked search results are targeted by SEO, but LLM answer engines create a new manipulable target for brand optimization.
layout: 2 parallel branches from one user query, left-to-right, color-coded yellow vs red
description: A user icon with question marks and the query "Best skincare products for moisture" sits on the left. Two arrows split from it. The top branch goes to a pale-yellow box with Google and Bing logos labeled "Traditional SEO". That leads to a yellow "Search Result" panel: a ranked list with a sponsored Ads banner at 1, then two brand tags at 2 and 3. The bottom branch goes to a blue-to-red gradient box with Gemini and ChatGPT logos and a robot icon. That leads to a red-gradient "LLM Answer" panel titled "Top-Rated Recommendations", with three ranked brand tags and a trophy icon. A small pink box labeled "GEO" sits below the LLM box. It shows a hacker figure pushing a brand tag upward into the LLM, with a warning triangle. The yellow vs red contrast carries the comparison.
caption: SEO targets search results, while GEO targets LLMs.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) answer engines are increasingly used for information seeking, shifting visibility from ranked lists to synthesized answers. This enables Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), which targets LLM answer engines' evidence pool and generation. We analyze the search engine optimization (SEO) to GEO transition to identify two risks: (i) concentrated influence from low contestability and system sensitivity, and (ii) undisclosed commercial influence embedded in evidence and reasoning. We then formalize a general GEO pipeline to locate where optimization acts and compare academic and industry practices, revealing a third risk: (iii) academic-industry blind spots driven by visibility and evaluation asymmetries between offline setups and deployed systems. This position argues the need for answer-level governance and measurement: stronger contestability, high-precision disclosure, black-box auditing of material influence, and deployment-aligned metrics for exposure persistence.
